item.title: Cache Stampede Mitigation in Redis Caching Strategies and Implementation of Redisson Distributed Locks
item.description:
In web application architectures centered on relational databases (RDBMS), disk I/O and connection pool exhaustion caused by sudden traffic spikes are factors that induce system-wide response delays and timeouts. Introducing Redis, an in-memory data store, as a caching layer can be expected to improve read performance; however, improper cache design or invalidation strategies risk triggering issues such as database load concentration caused by the expiration of specific keys (Cache Stampede) or data inconsistency during concurrent processing.

This article explains the selection criteria for major caching patterns, the implementation of distributed locks using Redisson, as well as Cache Stampede mitigation and memory management techniques in production operations.

1. Classification and Selection Criteria for Cache Patterns

An appropriate caching pattern must be selected based on data consistency requirements and write latency tolerance.

+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| CACHING PATTERNS |
+--------------------------+--------------------------+-----------------------------+
| Cache-Aside | Write-Through | Write-Back (Write-Behind) |
| (Read Optimization) | (Consistency First) | (Write Optimization) |
+--------------------------+--------------------------+-----------------------------+
| 1. App reads Cache | 1. App writes Cache | 1. App writes Cache only |
| 2. Miss -> Read DB | 2. Cache writes DB | 2. Async batch updates DB |
| 3. Populate Cache | (Synchronously) | |
+--------------------------+--------------------------+-----------------------------+

Cache-Aside (Look-Aside)

This is a common pattern aimed at optimizing read operations. The application queries Redis first; upon a cache miss, it retrieves data from the RDBMS and writes it back to Redis. Even if a Redis node fails, system availability is maintained because operations fall back to the database. However, a trade-off exists where requests hit the DB all at once when a hot key’s Time-To-Live (TTL) expires.

When updating data, the standard sequence is to “delete the Redis key after updating the DB,” but to prevent race conditions with concurrent reads, short-duration TTL settings or the Delayed Double Delete pattern must be considered.

Write-Through

During write operations, updates are performed synchronously to both the Redis cache and the RDBMS. High consistency between the cache and the database is maintained, allowing up-to-date data to be served constantly from the cache. On the other hand, latency increases because synchronous double writes occur for every write operation, and unreferenced data can also pressure cache memory capacity.

Write-Back (Write-Behind)

The application writes only to Redis and returns a response immediately. A background asynchronous process periodically commits changes to the RDBMS via batch processing. This is suitable for absorbing high-frequency write traffic, but if the Redis instance crashes before asynchronous processing completes, non-persisted data risks being permanently lost.

2. Implementation of Distributed Locks and Concurrency Control Using Redisson

Standard Java locks on a single instance (such as synchronized or ReentrantLock) do not function in a distributed application environment composed of multiple nodes. Furthermore, pessimistic locking in RDBMS (SELECT … FOR UPDATE) rapidly consumes connection pools under high concurrency and becomes a cause of deadlocks.

Redisson utilizes Redis’s single-threaded event loop and Pub/Sub event notification mechanism to provide safe distributed locks (RLock) while avoiding wasteful CPU consumption caused by spinlocks.

package com.example.service;

import org.redisson.api.RLock;
import org.redisson.api.RedissonClient;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;
import org.springframework.transaction.annotation.Transactional;

import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit;

@Service
public class StockService {

 private final RedissonClient redissonClient;
 private final ItemRepository itemRepository;

 public StockService(RedissonClient redissonClient, ItemRepository itemRepository) {
 this.redissonClient = redissonClient;
 this.itemRepository = itemRepository;
 }

 public void decreaseStock(Long itemId, int quantity) {
 RLock lock = redissonClient.getLock("stock:" + itemId);
 boolean acquired = false;
 try {
 // Wait up to 3 seconds for lock acquisition; automatically release 5 seconds after acquisition
 acquired = lock.tryLock(3, 5, TimeUnit.SECONDS);
 if (!acquired) {
 throw new IllegalStateException("Lock acquisition timed out for item: " + itemId);
 }
 // Execute the database transaction within the lock acquisition boundary
 executeDecreaseTransactional(itemId, quantity);
 } catch (InterruptedException e) {
 Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
 throw new RuntimeException("Thread interrupted during lock acquisition", e);
 } finally {
 if (acquired && lock.isLocked() && lock.isHeldByCurrentThread()) {
 lock.unlock();
 }
 }
 }

 @Transactional
 public void executeDecreaseTransactional(Long itemId, int quantity) {
 Item item = itemRepository.findById(itemId)
 .orElseThrow(() -> new IllegalArgumentException("Item not found: " + itemId));
 item.decrease(quantity);
 itemRepository.save(item);
 }
}

When operating distributed locks, if an explicit leaseTime is not specified in tryLock, Redisson activates the Watchdog feature, automatically extending the lock expiration to 30 seconds every 10 seconds as long as the thread remains alive.

3. Cache Stampede Avoidance and Production Operation Checklist

The phenomenon where a large number of threads simultaneously access the database and attempt to execute recomputations at the exact moment the TTL of a hot key heavily accessed by traffic expires is called a Cache Stampede.

Mitigation Strategies

  1. 💡 TTL Jitter (Adding Random Jitter): When setting the TTL for each key, dynamically add a random fluctuation of $\pm 10% \sim 20%$ to the base duration to disperse simultaneous expirations.

  2. 🛠️ Distributed Recomputation Lock (Single-Threaded Recomputation): Design the system so that upon a cache miss, only the single request that acquired the distributed lock retrieves data from the DB and performs recomputation, while other requests wait briefly or return stale cache data (Stale Payload).

  3. ⚠️ Probabilistic Early Recomputation (PER): Based on access frequency and recomputation cost, probabilistically calculate and update the cache in the background before the TTL completely expires.

Memory and Eviction Policy Optimization

・ Standardization of maxmemory Settings: If maxmemory is not set, there is a risk that the Redis process will be forcibly terminated by the OS OOM Killer.

・ Eviction Strategy Selection: Select volatile-lru when targeting only keys with a TTL configured, or allkeys-lru when targeting all keys as a dedicated cache layer. The use of noeviction in a cache layer is strictly prohibited.

・ Enforcement of Non-blocking Deletions: Using the synchronous command DEL when deleting keys with large data structures will halt single-threaded processing. Enforce the use of UNLINK, which performs asynchronous memory deallocation.

Troubleshooting

Inconsistency Between Transaction Boundaries and Lock Release (Dirty Reads)

If lock.unlock() is invoked inside a method annotated with @Transactional, the lock is released before the DB commit completes. If another thread acquires the lock at this precise moment, a race condition occurs where it references the uncommitted stale state. Lock acquisition and release must strictly be performed outside of DB transactions.

Exceptions Caused by Releasing Unowned Locks

If a thread’s lock has already been automatically released due to TTL expiration, executing unlock() on a lock owned by another thread throws an IllegalMonitorStateException. Always verify ownership using lock.isHeldByCurrentThread() prior to release.

System Verification Logs

Verify memory status and operational health in production environments periodically via CLI logs or similar means.

$ redis-cli info memory
# Memory
used_memory:268435456
used_memory_human:256.00M
used_memory_rss:314572800
used_memory_rss_human:300.00M
mem_fragmentation_ratio:1.17
mem_allocator:jemalloc-5.3.0

$ redis-cli slowlog get 5
1) 1) (integer) 12
 2) (integer) 1700000000
 3) (integer) 15200
 4) 1) "UNLINK"
 2) "stock:cache:1004"

$ redis-cli eval "return redis.call('ttl', KEYS[1])" 1 "stock:1001"
(integer) 298

Lessons Learned

In operating a highly concurrent caching infrastructure using Redis, it is indispensable not merely to use it as a data retention layer, but to comprehensively design for adding TTL jitter, concurrency control for recomputations, and memory overflow prevention measures (leveraging maxmemory and UNLINK). By implementing proper distributed lock boundary design and operational monitoring, stable operation with minimized DB load can be achieved even under high traffic conditions.

item.title: Redis Caching Strategies and Failure Mitigation Design in High-Load Web Environments
item.description:
In phases where web system traffic increases, the concentration of repetitive read queries against a relational database management system (RDBMS) becomes a primary factor leading to disk I/O saturation and database connection pool exhaustion. An architecture that relies solely on scaling up the storage layer inevitably suffers from deteriorating latency and escalating costs. To eliminate bottlenecks in highly concurrent environments, it is necessary to standardize a caching architecture that offloads read traffic by placing Redis, an in-memory data store, in front of the persistence layer.

This document compiles technical verification results regarding the rationale for adopting Redis in web infrastructure, selection criteria for key caching topologies, cache stampede prevention, and memory limit management.

Read Load Localization and Redis Characteristics

Because Redis retains and processes all data in main memory, it maintains sub-millisecond response latency compared to standard RDBMSs that involve disk seeks. Furthermore, its native support for diverse data structures—rather than operating merely as a simple key-value store—serves as an architectural advantage in system design.

  • String: Caching serialized object data and JSON strings
  • Hash: Structured retention of objects with multiple fields and discrete updates of specific fields
  • List / Set: Implementation of queue structures and unique user membership checks
  • Sorted Set (ZSet): Score-based real-time aggregation and sliding-window rate limiter implementations

By leveraging these data structures, Redis can do more than serve as a repository for query results; it can efficiently consolidate distributed infrastructure responsibilities such as session persistence and rate limiting.

Cache Pattern Design and Trade-offs

A cache access pattern suited to the requirements must be defined by balancing data consistency, fault tolerance, and overall system complexity.

Cache-Aside (Lazy Loading) Pattern 

+--------+ 1. Read Request +-----------------+
| Client | ------------------------> | Application |
+--------+ +-----------------+
 | ^
 2. Check Cache | | 5. Return Data
 v |
 +-------+ |
 | Redis | ---------+
 +-------+ (Cache Hit)
 |
 Cache Miss | 3. Query DB
 v
 +-------+
 | RDBMS |
 +-------+
 |
 4. Set Cache (TTL) |
 v
 +-------+
 | Redis |
 +-------+

In the Cache-Aside pattern, the application first queries Redis for data. If the cache exists (Cache Hit), that value is returned immediately to the client. If the cache does not exist (Cache Miss), data is fetched from the backend RDBMS, written to Redis with a TTL, and then returned in the response.

A key characteristic of this pattern is that even if a Redis node temporarily goes down, total service outage can be avoided as long as the application maintains fallback to the RDBMS. In addition, because only requested data is loaded into the cache, the memory footprint is kept to a minimum.

Write-Through and Write-Back Patterns

  • Write-Through: The application writes to the cache, and the cache layer performs a synchronous write to the RDBMS within the same transaction. While data consistency is ensured, dual write overhead occurs for every update operation.
  • Write-Back (Write-Behind): Writes are executed only to Redis, and a response is returned immediately. Persistence to the underlying storage layer is flushed asynchronously in batches by a background process. While this maximizes write throughput, it entails the risk of losing unflushed data if the Redis instance crashes abnormally.

Fault Tolerance Design and Operational Countermeasures

Mitigating Cache Stampede (Thundering Herd)

The moment the TTL of an extremely high-traffic key expires, numerous concurrent worker threads detect a Cache Miss simultaneously and issue identical queries concurrently to the RDBMS. This causes a sudden spike in database CPU utilization and cascades into connection timeouts.

To prevent this issue, fixed-value TTL configurations should be avoided, and expiration times configured with randomized variation (Jitter) should be introduced.

import random
import time
import redis

client = redis.Redis(host='127.0.0.1', port=6379, db=0)

def get_user_profile(user_id: str):
 cache_key = f"user:{user_id}:profile"
 cached_data = client.get(cache_key)
 
 if cached_data is not None:
 return cached_data.decode('utf-8')
 
 # Database fallback simulation
 db_data = fetch_from_database(user_id)
 
 # Base TTL: 3600 seconds, Jitter: 0-300 seconds
 base_ttl = 3600
 jitter = random.randint(0, 300)
 effective_ttl = base_ttl + jitter
 
 client.setex(cache_key, effective_ttl, db_data)
 return db_data

def fetch_from_database(user_id: str) -> str:
 return f"{{\"id\": \"{user_id}\", \"status\": \"active\"}}"

Probabilistically dispersing the TTL reduces the risk of all requests executing the fallback process simultaneously.

Memory Exhaustion (OOM) Countermeasures and Eviction Policies

Continuing operations without configuring an upper limit on cache capacity leads to excessive host memory consumption, triggering process termination by the OS OOM Killer or new write errors. The physical memory limit and eviction policy must be explicitly specified in redis.conf.

# Maximum memory allocation limit
maxmemory 2147483648

# Eviction policy settings
# Available: volatile-lru, allkeys-lru, volatile-lfu, allkeys-lfu, noeviction
maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru

# LRU / LFU sampling precision
maxmemory-samples 5
  • allkeys-lru: Evicts keys starting from the least recently used. Suitable for general web workloads adhering to the Pareto principle.
  • allkeys-lfu: Evaluates access frequency using a logarithmic access counter and evicts low-frequency keys. Useful for preventing keys accessed in transient one-off bursts from being retained.
  • noeviction: The default setting, where write operations return an OOM command not allowed error when the memory limit is reached. This behavior should be avoided when using Redis as a temporary caching layer.

Troubleshooting

1. OOM Error Upon Reaching Memory Limit

Symptom: The following errors occur continuously on the application side during SET operations to Redis.

(error) OOM command not allowed when used memory > 'maxmemory'.

Root Cause Analysis: maxmemory-policy remained configured as noeviction, and additions of new keys or data updates were attempted while the limit had been reached.

Action Taken: Issued the CONFIG SET command to the running Redis instance to dynamically change the eviction policy, followed by persisting the change to the configuration file.

redis-cli config set maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru
redis-cli config rewrite

2. Connection Latency Due to TCP Connection Backlog Limitation

Symptom: During traffic spikes, connection establishment latency to Redis increases, and Connection Timeouts are logged on the client side.

Root Cause Analysis: Occurs when the kernel’s socket listen backlog setting (net.core.somaxconn) is low and cannot accommodate Redis’s tcp-backlog (default: 511).

Action Taken: Modify kernel parameters on the host OS to expand the socket queue length.

sudo sysctl -w net.core.somaxconn=2048
echo "net.core.somaxconn = 2048" | sudo tee -a /etc/sysctl.conf

Verification Results and Operational Status

To verify consistency in the infrastructure layer after applying the configurations, memory utilization, connection listeners, and eviction statistics of the Redis process were retrieved via the terminal.

$ redis-cli info memory
# Memory
used_memory:1845493760
used_memory_human:1.72G
used_memory_rss:1924526080
used_memory_rss_human:1.79G
maxmemory:2147483648
maxmemory_human:2.00G
maxmemory_policy:allkeys-lru
mem_fragmentation_ratio:1.04

$ redis-cli info stats | grep evicted
evicted_keys:142095

$ ss -tulpn | grep 6379
tcp LISTEN 0 2048 127.0.0.1:6379 0.0.0.0:* users:(("redis-server",pid=10421,fd=6))

It was confirmed that used_memory was maintained within the configured 2.00GB limit, and that autonomous memory boundary management under the allkeys-lru policy functioned properly as evidenced by the increase in evicted_keys.

Operational Notes

Deploying a Redis cache as a single instance is an approach that offers immediate efficacy in mitigating RDBMS read load. However, to prevent the caching layer itself from becoming a single point of failure (SPOF), implementing redundant failover mechanisms is mandatory in subsequent operational phases.

As future milestones, it is necessary to build a highly fault-tolerant data platform by verifying Redis cluster configurations utilizing StatefulSets in Kubernetes environments, as well as automatic master failover mechanisms using Sentinel.
